# Fitting models

The goal is to assign each 48×48 face to one of four emotions: anger, disgust, happiness or sadness. 
We evaluate models by **classification accuracy**, the share of images classified correctly. As mentioned in the introduction of the notebook, 
humans reach about **74.4%** accuracy on this task, so we expect to do better than that with machine learning using the features
we've built in section 3. 
 
We compare three statistcial models, ordered from least to most flexible:

1. **Lasso multinomial logistic regression**
2. **Random forest**: 
3. **Support vector machine with a radial kernel**

Looking at both less and more flexible models allows us to see how the bias–variance trade-off plays out in practice. A less flexible method has 
higher bias (it cannot follow the true class boundaries closely) but lower variance (it is less sensitive to the particular training images).
 Which effect dominates depends on the data, so we cannot tell in
advance which method will have the highest test accuracy. Instead, we estimate it.

**How we measure performance.** We estimate test accuracy with 5-fold
cross-validation, with the folds grouped by subject. We do thisThe file names
start with a subject ID (`S005`, `S010`, ...), and `caret::groupKFold()` puts all images
of one person in the same fold. Each held-out fold therefore contains only people the model has not seen during training. 
This matters because the training set contains augmented copies of images and
neighbouring frames from the same video, which are nearly identical. With random
folds, near-duplicates of the same face would end up in both the training and the
validation folds. The model could then score well by recognising the person rather than
the expression, and the cross-validation estimate of the test accuracy might be too
optimistic. All three models use the same `folds` object, so
differences in cross-validated accuracy come from the models, not from different splits.

All models are trained on the built features from Section 3: feature-construction (`features_train`), not on the 2,304 raw pixels.
The features summarize shapes, edges and brightness in the facial regions that differ between expressions.

```{r classification-functions, code=readLines("R/evaluation/classification.R"), fold="Classification evaluation function", message=FALSE}
source("R/evaluation/classification.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r resampling-settings}
set.seed(2023)
subjects <- sub("_.*", "", basename(rownames(x_train)))
folds <- caret::groupKFold(subjects, k = 5)
control <- caret::trainControl("cv", 5, index = folds, allowParallel = TRUE)
models <- list()
```

## Lasso multinomial logistic regression

The first model is multinomial logistic regression with an lasso
penalty on the coefficients. It models the log-odds between each pair of
emotions as a linear function of the features. We start with the lasso model because we 
have many engineered features compared with the number of
subjects, so an unpenalized model would have high variance. The lasso penalty shrinks
the coefficients towards zero and sets some of them to exactly zero. This both selects a
smaller set of features and reduces variance. Because its decision boundaries are linear
in the features, it is the least flexible of our three models and serves as a baseline.

### Parameters
The penalty strength λ controls the flexibility of the model. A larger λ sets more
coefficients to zero, which lowers variance but raises bias. With λ = 0 we get ordinary
multinomial logistic regression. λ is chosen by cross-validation, where we try a grid of 20 values from 1 down
to 0.0001 and pick the one with the highest accuracy on our subject-grouped folds.
We use this best λ rather than the one-standard-error rule, because our goal is prediction accuracy rather than the simplest model.

The features are standardized before fitting, so that each has standard deviation one.
A feature measured on a large scale needs only a small coefficient, so it would be
penalized less than a feature measured on a small scale. Standardizing puts all
features on an equal footing. `glmnet()` does this by default.

```{r lasso-function, code=readLines("R/models/lasso.R"), fold="Lasso function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/lasso.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-lasso}
set.seed(2023)
models$lasso <- fit_lasso(features_train, y, control)
lasso <- models$lasso

lasso$bestTune # which lambda was chosen by cross-validation
lasso$results # Accuracy and Accuracy SD for chosen lambda
caret::confusionMatrix(lasso) # which emotions get confused, and Accuracy per class
```

### Results
### Results

Cross-validation selected λ = [LAMBDA]. The model reached a cross-validated accuracy of
[CV_ACC]% (SD across folds: [CV_SD] percentage points), which is [ABOVE/BELOW] the human
benchmark of 74.4%. Most errors came from confusing [EMOTION_A] with [EMOTION_B], while
[EMOTION_C] was recognised best ([CLASS_ACC]% correct).

The lasso's decision boundaries are linear and additive in the features, so it cannot
capture interactions such as "brows lowered *and* mouth closed" unless we add them by
hand. Tree-based methods pick up such interactions and non-linear effects automatically.

## Random forest
A single classification tree would be the simplest tree-based option, but it has high
variance. A small change in the training data can produce a very different tree, and
single trees are usually less accurate than other methods. A random
forest addresses this. It grows many trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training
images, and classifies an image by majority vote, and thus averaging many trees reduces the
variance. In addition, at each split a tree may only choose from a fresh random subset of m of
the p features, which ends up decorrelating the trees. Without it, most trees would split on the
same few strong features first and look very similar, and averaging similar trees
reduces the variance much less. This suits our features well. Many of them are strongly correlated, 
for example the HOG features of the same region computed on 2×2 and 4×4 grids. 

### Parameters
The number of features per split, m (`mtry`), controls how different the trees are.
We consider m = √p features at each split, the standard choice for classification,
which makes the trees clearly different from each other while still giving each split
enough features to choose a good one.
The number of trees, B (`ntree`), does not cause overfitting as it grows, but it only needs
to be large enough for the error to settle down. Thus we choose to use B = 300.
We stop splitting a node once it contains 10 or fewer images (`min.node.size = 10`).
This keeps the individual trees somewhat shallower and less flexible, while the
averaging over trees keeps the variance under control.

```{r forest-function, code=readLines("R/models/random_forest.R"), fold="Random forest function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/random_forest.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-forest}
set.seed(2023)
models$forest <- fit_random_forest(features_train, y, control)
forest <- models$forest

forest$results # m, Accuracy and , Accuracy SD
caret::confusionMatrix(forest) # which emotions get confused, and Accuracy per class
```
### Results

With B = 300 trees, m = [MTRY] features per split and a minimum node size of 10, the
random forest reached a cross-validated accuracy of [CV_ACC]% (SD across folds:
[CV_SD] percentage points). This is [GAIN] percentage points [higher/lower] than the
lasso and [ABOVE/BELOW] the human benchmark of 74.4%. [This suggests that interactions
and non-linear effects in the features carry useful information that the lasso missed. /
The extra flexibility did not pay off, which suggests that a linear boundary already
captures most of the information in our features.] Most errors came from confusing
[EMOTION_A] with [EMOTION_B], while [EMOTION_C] was recognised best ([CLASS_ACC]% correct).


Each tree split uses only one feature at a time, so a random forest builds its decision
boundaries from axis-aligned steps and struggles to approximate smooth boundaries that
depend on many features at once. [If anger, disgust and sadness are still
often confused,] a support vector machine with a radial kernel is a natural next step,
since it fits a smooth non-linear boundary in the full feature space.

## Radial SVM
We choose to implement a Rdical SVM instead of a support vector classifier with a linear boundary. 
Its loss function is very similar to that of logistic regression, so the two often give very similar 
results, and the lasso already covers a linear boundary for us.

Instead, we use a support vector machine with a radial kernel. Like the support vector
classifier, it looks for a boundary with a wide margin between the classes, but allows
some images to fall on the wrong side of the margin. The radial kernel makes the boundary non-linear. 
It is also local: an image is classified mainly by the training images that are close to it in the feature space, while distant
images play almost no role. For our four emotions, `e1071::svm()` uses the
one-versus-one approach. It fits an SVM for each of the six pairs of emotions and
assigns each image to the emotion that wins most of these pairwise votes..

### Parameters
`cost` sets how much a violation of the margin is penalised. A large cost gives a
narrow margin with few violations, and thus also a more flexible boundary with lower bias but higher
variance. We use cost = 4.
`gamma` (γ) sets how local the radial kernel is. A larger γ means that
only very close training images influence a prediction, which makes the boundary more
non-linear and risks overfitting. Because the kernel sums squared
differences over all p features, distances grow with the number of
features. We thus scale γ with p and use γ = 0.1/p.
Before fitting, we remove features that are constant and centre and scale the rest
(`preProcess`), which is done within each training fold. As with the lasso, scaling
matters because the radial kernel is based on distances between images, so features
measured on a large scale would otherwise dominate.

```{r svm-function, code=readLines("R/models/radial_svm.R"), fold="Radial SVM function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/radial_svm.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-svm}
set.seed(2023)
models$svm_radial <- fit_radial_svm(features_train, y, control)
radial_svm <- models$svm_radial
radial_svm$results # CV accuracy and its SD
caret::confusionMatrix(radial_svm) # which emotions get confused
```

### Results
With cost = 4 and γ = 0.1/p, the radial SVM reached a cross-validated accuracy of
[CV_ACC]% (SD across folds: [CV_SD] percentage points). This is [GAIN_RF] percentage
points [higher/lower] than the random forest and [GAIN_LASSO] percentage points
[higher/lower] than the lasso, and [ABOVE/BELOW] the human benchmark of 74.4%.
[This suggests that a smooth non-linear boundary in the full feature space separates
the emotions better than the forest's axis-aligned splits. / The smooth boundary did not
improve on the forest, which suggests that the axis-aligned splits already capture the
relevant non-linear structure in our features.] Most errors came from confusing
[EMOTION_A] with [EMOTION_B], while [EMOTION_C] was recognised best ([CLASS_ACC]% correct).

## Comparing the models
Because all three models were evaluated on the same subject-grouped folds, we can
compare their cross-validated accuracies directly. The table below lists each model's
mean accuracy over the five folds and its training time, sorted from best to worst.

```{r compare-models}
# Compare models on the same folds
resampling <- caret::resamples(models)
model_comparison <- summary(resampling)$statistics$Accuracy |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("model") |>
  select(model, accuracy = Mean) |>
  mutate(seconds = sapply(models[model], function(m) m$times$everything[["elapsed"]])) |>
  arrange(dplyr::desc(accuracy))
model_comparison
```

As always, it's useful to check how well the algorithm performs on the training set: If
it doesn't classify the training set accurately, how can you expect better results on
the test set? This seemingly obvious point is often overlooked—surprisingly.

```{r evaluate-models}
cat("Evaluating models on training set...\n")
training_performance <- lapply(models, function(model) {
  predictions <- predict(model, features_train, type = "raw")
  evaluate_classification(predictions, y)
})
training_performance
```

On the training set, the lasso classified [TRAIN_LASSO]% of the images correctly, the
random forest [TRAIN_RF]% and the radial SVM [TRAIN_SVM]%, compared with cross-validated
accuracies of [CV_LASSO]%, [CV_RF]% and [CV_SVM]%. [None of the models underfits badly. /
The lasso already struggles on the training images, which points to high bias.] The gap
between training and cross-validated accuracy is [GAP_LASSO] percentage points for the
lasso, [GAP_RF] for the forest and [GAP_SVM] for the SVM. [As expected from the
bias–variance trade-off, the gap grows with flexibility: the more flexible models fit the
training images more closely, but part of that fit does not carry over to new subjects. /
Unlike what the bias–variance trade-off would suggest, the gap does not grow with
flexibility, which suggests that ...] For the forest, a high training accuracy is
expected anyway, since its trees are grown deep. We therefore choose between the models
by their cross-validated accuracy, not their training accuracy (Section 5).
